en: The Sutra of the Nine-Colored Deer Spoken by the Buddha, one fascicle;
translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu Dynasty.
Long ago, the Bodhisattva was born as a nine-colored deer; its fur was of nine different colors, and its antlers were white.
Like a crane, he constantly dwelt by the banks of the Ganges, feeding on water plants and grasses, and had long been a companion to a crow.
At that time, a drowning man came floating down the current; now surfacing and now submerging, he managed to grasp a tree branch and looked up toward heaven, crying out:
"O mountain spirits, tree spirits, and all you devas and nāga-spirits, why do you not take pity on me?"
Hearing the sound of people, the deer went into the water and said to the drowning man, "Do not be afraid!
You may mount my back and grasp both my horns; I shall carry you out of the water."
Having reached the shore, the deer was utterly exhausted; the man who had been drowning went down to the ground, circumambulated the deer three times, and prostrated himself before it, saying:
"I beg to become a slave to you, my master, to provide for you and serve you by gathering water and grass."
The deer said, "I have no need for you;
each of you should depart for now. If you wish to repay my kindness, do not say that I am here; people covet my hide and antlers, and they will surely come to kill me."
Thereupon, the man who had drowned accepted the instruction and departed.

At that time, while the king’s consort was sleeping at night, she saw in a dream a nine-colored deer; its fur was of nine different colors and its horns were white as snow. She immediately feigned illness and did not rise from her bed.
The king asked the lady,
"For what reason do you not rise? She replied:
"Last night I dreamed of an extraordinary deer; its fur was nine colors and its antlers were white as snow.
I thought of obtaining its hide to make a sitting mat and its antlers to make a fly-whisk handle. Would Your Majesty seek it out for me?"
"If Your Majesty does not obtain it, I shall die.
The King said to his consort:
"You may rise for now; as the sovereign of a kingdom, what is there that I cannot obtain?"
The king immediately issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom:

"If there is anyone who can find the nine-colored deer, I shall share my kingdom with him to rule; I will grant him a golden bowl filled with silver grain, and also a silver bowl filled with golden grain."
Thereupon, the drowning man, hearing of the king’s heavy reward, conceived an evil thought:
"I said that by killing this deer I could obtain wealth and status; but the deer is a mere beast—what does it matter whether it lives or dies?"
Thereupon, the drowning man spoke to the recruiters, saying,
"I know the whereabouts of the nine-colored deer.
The recruiters then led the drowning man to the Great King and addressed him, saying:
"This man knows the whereabouts of the nine-colored deer.
Upon hearing these words, the king was greatly delighted and said to the drowning man:
"If you can find the nine-colored deer, I shall grant you half of my kingdom; these words are not false."
The diver replied to the king,
"I can obtain it. Thereupon,
a leprous sore immediately broke out on the diver's face.
The drowning man said to the king, "Although this deer is but an animal, it possesses great majestic power; Your Majesty should dispatch a large number of men, and only then may you capture it."
The king immediately mobilized a great army and proceeded to the banks of the Ganges.
At that time, the crow, seeing the king’s army approaching from atop a tree, suspected they intended to kill the deer;
he then called out to the deer, saying, "Friend, arise at once!"
"The King has come to take you away.
The deer still did not wake; the crow then descended from the tree, perched upon its head, and pecked at its ear, saying:
"Friend, arise at once!"
"The King's army has arrived!

The deer, startled, immediately looked around in all four directions; seeing the King's host already encircling him a hundred times with no place left to flee, he went straight before the King's chariot.
At that time, the king’s soldiers immediately drew their bows, intending to shoot; the deer spoke to the king’s men, saying:
"Do not shoot me yet. I shall come to the king's presence myself, for I have something to say."
The king then commanded his ministers:
"Do not shoot this deer; this is no ordinary deer, for it may be a celestial deity.
The deer spoke again to the great king, saying:
"Do not kill me! I have rendered great service to this kingdom.
The king spoke thus to the deer.
"What kindness have you done for me?
the deer replied, "Previously,
I saved one person within Your Majesty’s kingdom."
The deer then knelt down on its hind legs and asked the king again, "Who said I was here?
The king then pointed out that it was the man with the leprous face by the chariot.
Hearing the king’s words, tears welled up in the deer’s eyes and it could not restrain itself;
the deer said, “Great King!
This man was submerged in deep water the day before yesterday and was carried downstream by the current. Emerging and submerging, he managed to grasp a tree and looked up, calling out to Heaven:”
"O mountain deities, tree deities, and all you devas and nāgas, why do you not take pity on me?

At that time, I did not spare my own life or body; I threw myself into the water to carry this person out. Originally, I had vowed not to speak of it to others, yet this man was ungrateful—worse than carrying a piece of floating wood in the water.
Upon hearing the deer’s words, the king was deeply ashamed and reproached his subjects, saying:
"Having received such great kindness from another, how could you instead wish to kill them?"
Thereupon, the Great King immediately issued an edict throughout the kingdom:
"From this day forward, should anyone drive away this deer, I shall execute his family for five generations."

Thereupon, several thousand deer gathered in herds and all came to depend upon him; they consumed water and grass without encroaching upon the crops. The winds and rains were timely, the five grains ripened in abundance, people suffered no illnesses, and calamities did not arise; the world was at peace until his life’s span ended and he passed away.
The Buddha said:
"The nine-colored deer at that time was my own self;
the crow at that time is now Ānanda."
The king at that time was the present King Śuddhodana;
the king’s consort at that time was the present Gautamī;
and the man who drowned at that time was the present Devadatta.
Devadatta and I have harbored enmity throughout successive lifetimes; though I have maintained a virtuous disposition toward him, he has nevertheless sought to harm me.
Ānanda, however, possesses a most sincere intention and shall attain the Unsurpassed Way.
"When the Bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), his forbearance is such as this.
The *Sūtra of the Nine-Colored Deer*, translated by the Buddha, in one fascicle.
